# Song of Solomon 6: research notes

**Coverage.** I used up my search budget before reaching several sites, so I have no notes from Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) or Catholic and Orthodox commentary (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org). I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching for this chapter. Below, "tradition" labels describe the commentator, not the website. Many Bible Hub and StudyLight pages gather several commentators on one page. Where a snippet didn't name its author, I've said so rather than guess.

**The main split runs through the whole chapter.** It is less between denominations than between ways of reading the book:
- **Literal (marriage) reading:** a husband and wife making up after a quarrel. Guzik and Constable read it this way.
- **Allegorical reading:** Christ and the church. Gill, Matthew Henry, JFB, Trapp, the Geneva Bible and Chuck Smith read it this way.
- **Three-character reading:** a shepherd and King Solomon competing for the maiden. Coffman reads it this way.

---

**v. 1**
- **Literal:** It's unclear whether the women are supportive or sarcastic. Having heard her praise of him, they want to help find him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
- **Literal:** The Shulammite convinced the daughters of Jerusalem that her love for her husband was deep and genuine. They agreed to search for Solomon with her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Allegorical (Gill, Baptist):** They were not just curious. They meant to join the church in seeking Christ in the word and ordinances. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Allegorical (Matthew Henry):** People undervalue Christ because they don't know him. Her love scattered sparks into theirs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/6-3.html
- **Literary (Ellicott):** The poet uses the bystanders' reaction to heighten his picture of the lover's beauty. Ellicott thinks this passage causes real problems for the "drama" theory. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html

**v. 2**
- **Disputed: what "garden" means.**
  - Guzik notes that "garden" stood for the maiden's sexuality earlier in the book, but thinks a literal garden fits better here. She remembers where he would be: tending his flock and gathering lilies for her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
  - Utley reads the garden as the maiden herself, and the line as a euphemism for lovemaking. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/song-of-solomon-6.html
- Another view on preceptaustin: the garden is the king's work, the flock is the people; the lilies represent the produce of the land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary_6
- Constable links it to Solomon's love of gardens (Ecclesiastes 2:5) and suggests the knowledge of where he was came to her in her dream. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Three-character reading (Coffman, Churches of Christ):** Coffman rejects Solomon as gardener or shepherd and concludes the maiden's lover is clearly a shepherd, the Shepherd. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/song-of-solomon-6.html

**v. 3**
- **Literal:** Remembering who he is restores her sense of oneness with him. Guzik's point is that the breakthrough came from thinking, not feelings. He also notes the reversal from 2:16: "he is mine" becomes "I am his," as if belonging to him now mattered more than having him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
- **Allegorical:**
  - Gill: the words express her union with Christ and her faith, which still continued, notwithstanding her unbecoming behavior toward Christ. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/song-of-solomon/6-3.html
  - Henry also comments on the reversed order: first she is wholly devoted to him, then she claims him as hers. Even without felt comfort, she holds on to "Christ is mine and I am his." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/6-3.html
- Utley takes the verse as her trust in his faithfulness and adds that this surely does not fit Solomon. https://bible.org/seriespage/song-songs-6

**v. 4**
- **Tirzah:**
  - Guzik, quoting Kinlaw, says naming Tirzah, the northern capital before Samaria, points to an early date. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
  - Ellicott says the two cities are paired only because both were capitals, of the northern and southern kingdoms. He uses this to date the poem and notes that ancient versions translated "Tirzah" as a common noun. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - JFB argues the opposite of a late date: Tirzah was already the northern capital in Solomon's time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Sgs/Sgs_006.cfm
- **Literal (Guzik):** He forgives quickly and with no bitterness, even though the break was mostly her fault. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
- **"Army with banners":**
  - Constable: Solomon probably felt weak at the knees at her beauty, as he would facing an army. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Gill: the army image shows that a group is meant, not one person. The church on earth is militant and fearsome to Satan and false teachers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Spurgeon (Baptist), as summarised by Guzik: the church carries banners to show its identity, discipline, readiness for action and confidence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
  - Coffman: the maiden's purity and faithfulness have rebuked the king and his artificial flattery. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/song-of-solomon-6.html

**v. 5**
- **Literal (Guzik):** High praise, as if he can't bear how beautiful her eyes are. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
- **Hebrew (Ellicott):** The verb may mean "make me bold." The Septuagint, the Vulgate and many modern scholars take it as "scare" or "dazzle." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Allegorical:**
  - Gill lists several renderings and says Christ takes a kind of pride in the graces he has worked in his church, especially her faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Spurgeon, via Guzik: Jesus is "overcome" by eyes that repent, mourn over sin, look to him and pray. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/

**vv. 5b–7 (repeating 4:1–3)**
- **Literal (Guzik):** He repeats his wedding-night praise to say he values her as much as ever. He deliberately leaves out her more sensual features so she won't think he only wants to make up for the sake of sex. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
- **Allegorical (JFB):** The repetition is not empty. It shows his love is unchanged after her temporary unfaithfulness (Malachi 3:6). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Sgs/Sgs_006.cfm
- **Historical survey:** Some Christian interpreters applied the two descriptions to the church in different eras. Jewish interpreters applied them to Israel under the first and second temples. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/6-8.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- **Who are the queens and concubines? (literal)**
  - Guzik sets out three possibilities for how this fits Solomon's later 700 wives. He cites Carr's point that the text says "there are," not "I have." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
  - Ellicott takes it as Solomon's harem, with more modest numbers than 1 Kings 11:3. He sees verse 9 as a eulogy on monogamy-style praise of one wife. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Constable's source suggests that if the marriage was monogamous, these women belonged to the court, not his own harem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Coffman, by contrast, says Solomon is clearly meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/6-6.html
- **Literal application (Guzik):** It matters for a wife to feel preferred above all others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/
- **Allegorical: what the women stand for.** Readings differ even within the Reformed and Baptist line:
  - Gill gives three options: the nations, false churches (naming Rome, Arians and Socinians), or, his preference, believers at different stages. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/gnt/song-of-solomon/6-8.html
  - JFB: rulers of the earth, contrasted with the saints, who are many but one bride. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/6-8.htm
  - Poole: possibly local congregations and individual believers, together making one catholic (universal) church. Same page.
  - Geneva Bible: the endless gifts Christ gives his church, or the great number of the faithful. Same page.
- **"My dove… is one":** Gill says this means the church's small number or its unity: one body, one Spirit, one Head. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html

**v. 10**
- **Who speaks?** Ellicott gives the words to the admiring ladies. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** The Hebrew word for moon literally means "the white one." The NET notes compare this string of images to the praise of Simon the high priest in Sirach 50. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=sos&chapter=6&verse=10
- **Allegorical:**
  - Gill reads the moon as the church under the Old Testament ceremonial law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/6-10.html
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): the moon only reflects light, so the church reflects Christ's light. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/6-10.html
  - Geneva Bible: the church started small and grew great. https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/jvl/song-of-solomon/6-10.html
- **A Protestant–Catholic dispute (Trapp, Puritan):** Trapp uses the moon's waxing and waning against the Catholic teaching that the church is always visible. He argues that, like the moon, the true church can be hidden or eclipsed by persecution. https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/jvl/song-of-solomon/6-10.html

**v. 11**
- **Who speaks?**
  - Constable thinks it is probably her. She went to see whether his love was still blooming more than to look at plants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Gill gives the words to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Literal (Guzik):** Spring is returning, a sign their love is in springtime again. Guzik quotes Watchman Nee's reading of the "nuts" as God's Word as an example of over-spiritualising. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-6/

**v. 12**
- **Text problems (Ellicott):** He gives a word-for-word rendering, shows that the Septuagint and Vulgate read it differently, and concludes the Hebrew text has not come down to us intact. He warns against building a whole drama on this verse. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Constable:** His words of love lifted her spirits, as if she commanded Solomon's chariots. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Everett:** Many modern translations take it as being drawn back to her homeland. Garrett and others read it as being carried off in the king's chariot to a new life as his wife. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Gill:** He leaves open whether the church or Christ is speaking. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html

**v. 13**
- **"Shulammite":**
  - Ellicott: most likely "girl from Shunem." He calls the idea that it is a feminine form of "Solomon" untenable. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Utley lists several theories, including "perfect one" and a place name. He thinks a goddess origin is most unlikely. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Gill takes it as the bride sharing the name of Christ, "the true Solomon," and meaning both perfection and peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **"Dance of Mahanaim": sharply disputed.**
  - Ellicott says linking it to Jacob's angels (Genesis 32:2) borders on the absurd. He suggests a wedding sword-dance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Other commentators on the same Bible Hub page disagree with each other:
    - One reads it as an "angelic" sight.
    - Another links it to Jacob prevailing in prayer and sees her warfare between flesh and spirit.
    - A third thinks it was a famous sacred dance held at Mahanaim.
    https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/6-13.htm
  - Gill: she means nothing can be seen in her but two armies, sin and grace, at war (Romans 7:23). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/song-of-solomon-6.html
- **Literal:**
  - Constable: Solomon answers the crowd. He notes there is no record of any such event at Mahanaim. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/song-of-solomon-6.html
  - Guzik: the phrase suggests she was dancing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-7/
- **Bible Hub notes:** Her question challenges the onlookers' motives. In the literal sense it protects married love from being made a public show. In the spiritual sense it warns the church to keep her devotion to Christ reverent. https://biblehub.com/songs/6-13.htm
